results.title: Ai Validation Methods → Term
results.content:
Title: Ai Validation Methods → Term
Thus, the origin of AI validation within sustainability is deeply intertwined with ethical considerations and the precautionary principle → the mandate to anticipate and mitigate potential harm, especially when dealing with complex, adaptive systems like ecosystems and societies. Concurrently, the increasing deployment of AI in critical infrastructure and environmental monitoring highlighted the need for robust validation against adversarial attacks and distributional shifts → ensuring models perform reliably even when encountering unexpected or manipulated inputs, or when the underlying data patterns change over time (a constant in ecological systems). The ascendancy of AI validation methods within sustainability discourse is a direct consequence of AI’s deepening integration into ecologically and socially critical systems. | ~2018 onwards | Rise of “AI for Good” / AI for SDGs Initiatives | Explicitly focused research and application on sustainability challenges, driving the need for validation frameworks tailored to environmental and social impact assessment, beyond standard ML benchmarks. Today, especially in sustainability, validation must concurrently assess a portfolio of criteria: accuracy remains important, but so too are fairness (across different groups and regions), robustness (to changing conditions and adversarial inputs), interpretability (for stakeholder trust and scientific validity), efficiency (computational and energy costs), and alignment (ensuring the AI’s objective function genuinely reflects complex sustainability goals). This includes advancements in validating models under distributional shift (when the data patterns change over time, e.g., due to climate change), techniques for quantifying prediction uncertainty more reliably, and methods for validating AI agents operating within complex simulations of future environmental or socio-economic scenarios. The economic dimension of AI validation in sustainability examines the system’s contribution to **resource efficiency, sustainable economic models, and financial viability without compromising social or environmental integrity**. For AI in sustainable finance, validation focuses on the accuracy of ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) scoring, greenwashing detection, or climate risk assessment models. The significance of AI Validation Methods in the context of sustainability cannot be overstated; they serve as the crucial gatekeepers ensuring that powerful technological tools are deployed responsibly and effectively towards achieving ecological balance and social equity. Standardized protocols for validating AI across the diverse spectrum of sustainability applications (from ecological modeling to supply chain optimization to social impact assessment) are still nascent.

results.title: A Novel Method for Navigational Risk Assessment in Wind Farm Waters Based on the Fuzzy Inference System - Lv - 2021 - Mathematical Problems in Engineering - Wiley Online Library
results.content: Aiming at the problems that the navigational risk of ships in the waters of offshore wind farms is difficult to quantify due to complex factors, this paper proposes a method of navigational risk assessment in the waters of offshore wind farms based on a fuzzy inference system. Considering the mutual influence of the factors, the fuzzy inference rules of navigational risk influence are established according to the expert experience, and a method of navigational risk assessment based on the fuzzy inference system in offshore wind farm waters is developed. Based on the analysis of factors affecting ship navigation in wind farm waters, a fuzzy inference model is established by extracting factors such as the number of traffic flows, the number of meeting areas, and the distance between the sailing route and the wind farm. In order to quantitatively analyze the navigational risk of offshore wind farm waters, this paper extracts 6 influencing factors closely related to the overall navigational risk as input indexes and designs the model of navigational risk assessment in offshore wind farm waters based on the fuzzy inference system, as shown in Figures 7 and 8. The comprehensive FIS is established based on the comprehensive consideration of the influence of natural condition sailing risk and navigational environment sailing risk on the overall navigational risk, and the obtained natural condition sailing risk “3” and navigational environment sailing risk “5” are input into the comprehensive fuzzy inference system, and the navigational risk of ships in the whole Changle offshore wind farm area of Fujian is finally obtained as “5.” These are “high-risk” navigational waters, as shown in Figure 15. The above analysis shows that the evaluation method studied in this paper is feasible, and the fuzzy inference system can effectively calculate the navigational risk in the waters of offshore wind farms, and the calculated results meet the actual situation, thus verifying the rationality of the model. Considering the mutual influence of several factors, combined with the expert experience and established fuzzy inference rules, then finally the framework of navigational risk assessment based on the fuzzy inference system in offshore wind farm waters is formed.

Title: A Fuzzy-FMEA Risk Assessment Approach for Offshore Wind Turbines
							| International Journal of Prognostics and Health Management
## A Fuzzy-FMEA Risk Assessment Approach for Offshore Wind Turbines. ## ##plugins.themes.bootstrap3.article.main##. ## ##plugins.themes.bootstrap3.article.sidebar##. ## Abstract. Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) has been extensively used by wind turbine assembly manufacturers for risk and reliability analysis. However, several limitations are associated with its implementation in offshore wind farms: (i) the failure data gathered from SCADA system is often missing or unreliable, and hence, the assessment information of the three risk factors (i.e., severity, occurrence, and fault detection) are mainly based on experts’ knowledge; (ii) it is rather difficult for experts to precisely evaluate the risk factors; (iii) the relative importance among the risk factors is not taken into consideration, and hence, the results may not necessarily represent the true risk priorities; and etc. To overcome these drawbacks and improve the effectiveness of the traditional FMEA, we develop a fuzzy-FMEA approach for risk and failure mode analysis in offshore wind turbine systems. The information obtained from the experts is expressed using fuzzy linguistics terms, and a grey theory analysis is proposed to incorporate the relative importance of the risk factors into the determination of risk priority of failure modes. The proposed approach is applied to an offshore wind turbine system with sixteen mechanical, electrical and auxiliary assemblies, and the results are compared with the traditional FMEA. ## ##plugins.themes.bootstrap3.article.details##.
